supported_facts: BLS reported that the all-items CPI rose 2.3% over the 12 months ending April 2025 and 0.2% on a seasonally adjusted monthly basis.
The 12-month increase was lower than the 2.4% reported for the period ending March.
unsupported_original_claims: The frozen 4.2% April 2025 CPI figure is contradicted by the BLS release.
The release does not attribute the April CPI movement to tariffs or establish a tariff-driven inflation spike or stagflation event.
access_notes: The archived BLS CPI news release returned readable official text and reported both the monthly and annual changes.
narrow_corrected_title: BLS Reports April 2025 CPI Rose 2.3% Over 12 Months
narrow_corrected_claim: BLS reported that CPI rose 2.3% over the 12 months ending April 2025 and 0.2% from March on a seasonally adjusted basis. The release does not establish that tariffs caused the reported change.
exact_remaining_gap: The cited BLS release contradicts the stored 4.2% figure and does not support a causal claim that tariffs drove April inflation.

supported_facts: A George Washington University study commissioned by the Puerto Rico government estimated 2,975 excess deaths from September 2017 through February 2018 after Hurricane Maria.
The estimate is excess mortality compared with expected deaths; it is not a count of deaths individually attributed to federal response decisions.
unsupported_original_claims: The cited study does not attribute all 2,975 excess deaths to the Trump administration's actions or omissions.
The reviewed sources do not establish the frozen claims about the administration's initial 64-death count, Jones Act timing, or specific aid-distribution failures.
access_notes: GWU's report and its public statement returned readable text excerpts. The study describes an excess-mortality estimate and does not assign that estimate to federal conduct.
narrow_corrected_title: GWU Study Estimates 2,975 Excess Deaths in Puerto Rico After Hurricane Maria
narrow_corrected_claim: A George Washington University study commissioned by Puerto Rico estimated 2,975 excess deaths between September 2017 and February 2018 following Hurricane Maria. This is an excess-mortality estimate associated with the hurricane, not a study attribution of each death to the Trump administration's response.
exact_remaining_gap: The cited study does not establish that the administration caused the full estimated toll or substantiate the specific response failures and public statements in the frozen synopsis.

supported_facts: Reuters reported that on March 31, 2025, Planned Parenthood said nine affiliates had received notice that Title X family-planning funding would be withheld beginning April 1.
The report describes a Title X funding freeze affecting nine affiliates, not a termination of all federal funding to Planned Parenthood nationwide.
unsupported_original_claims: The frozen February date and claim that the administration eliminated all federal Planned Parenthood funding nationwide are unsupported by the cited report.
The source does not establish that all Medicaid reimbursements or every Title X grant were terminated.
access_notes: The Reuters article returned readable excerpts attributing the notification to Planned Parenthood and specifying nine affiliates and Title X.
narrow_corrected_title: Trump Administration Withholds Title X Funds From Nine Planned Parenthood Affiliates
narrow_corrected_claim: On March 31, 2025, Planned Parenthood said nine affiliates had been notified that Title X funding would be withheld beginning April 1. Reuters reported on the family-planning grant action; it does not show that all federal Planned Parenthood funding was eliminated nationwide.
exact_remaining_gap: The cited report does not support a February 2025 nationwide defunding event or a complete end to Medicaid reimbursements and all Title X funding.

supported_facts: AP reported on May 9, 2025 that the Pentagon directed military leaders and commands to review and pull library books addressing diversity, anti-racism, or gender issues by May 21.
The reported directive applied to military libraries; it was not a blanket order to all Title I or federally funded public schools.
unsupported_original_claims: The frozen February date and claim of a federal directive covering all federally funded school libraries are unsupported by this AP report.
The source does not establish that schools removed books or that the American Library Association, PEN America, or book-ban advocates responded to this military-library action.
access_notes: The AP report returned readable text identifying the Pentagon directive, its target libraries, subject matter, and deadline.
narrow_corrected_title: Pentagon Orders Military Libraries to Review Books on DEI Topics
narrow_corrected_claim: On May 9, 2025, AP reported that the Pentagon ordered military leaders and commands to review and pull library books addressing diversity, anti-racism, or gender issues by May 21. The reported order concerned military libraries, not all Title I schools.
exact_remaining_gap: The cited report does not support the frozen February event or a nationwide school-library mandate; implementation and any later legal challenges require separate documentation.

supported_facts: The Justice Department page states that President Trump granted clemency on January 20, 2025 for certain offenses relating to events at or near the Capitol on January 6, 2021.
The source identifies this as presidential clemency under a proclamation, rather than a January 21 instruction from Attorney General Pam Bondi to dismiss pending cases.
unsupported_original_claims: The frozen claim that Pam Bondi directed mass dismissals on January 21 is chronologically unsupported; she had not yet been confirmed as attorney general.
The proclamation does not support dismissals of unrelated pending criminal cases or the claim that the DOJ initiated partisan amnesty.
access_notes: The Justice Department Office of the Pardon Attorney page returned readable text and identifies the proclamation date and covered offenses.
narrow_corrected_title: Trump Grants Clemency for Certain January 6-Related Offenses
narrow_corrected_claim: On January 20, 2025, President Trump issued a proclamation granting clemency for certain offenses related to the January 6 Capitol events. The cited Justice Department source describes presidential pardons and commutations, not Bondi-directed dismissals of pending prosecutions.
exact_remaining_gap: The source does not establish a January 21 Bondi directive or dismissal of unrelated cases; any separate DOJ motions require case-specific records.

supported_facts: The January 20, 2025 executive orders directed agencies, to the extent allowed by law, to terminate environmental-justice offices, positions, plans, programs, and certain grants or contracts; another order revoked prior federal environmental-justice orders.
EPA announced on February 11 that it had placed 171 DEIA and environmental-justice employees on administrative leave.
unsupported_original_claims: The executive orders and EPA release do not establish that every environmental-justice program, office, employee, and grant was immediately terminated on January 20.
The sources do not support the claim that all relevant Biden-era rules and hundreds of millions of dollars in grants were canceled in that single January action.
access_notes: Both White House orders and EPA's February 11 release returned readable text. The orders direct agency actions; EPA's later release documents one agency implementation step.
narrow_corrected_title: Trump Orders Agencies to End Environmental-Justice Programs; EPA Later Places Staff on Leave
narrow_corrected_claim: On January 20, 2025, Trump signed orders directing agencies to end environmental-justice offices and programs to the extent allowed by law and revoking prior environmental-justice orders. EPA later said it had placed 171 DEIA and environmental-justice employees on administrative leave on February 11; that does not document a complete immediate shutdown of all federal programs.
exact_remaining_gap: The cited records do not establish that all programs, staff, rules, or grants were ended on January 20; agency-by-agency implementation and grant cancellations need separate evidence.

supported_facts: Reuters reported on April 25, 2025 that DOGE had ordered cancellation of around $400 million in AmeriCorps grants, citing the Washington Post.
Reuters reported on April 29 that states sued after grant-termination notices began and alleged the administration had cut 85% of the agency's workforce.
unsupported_original_claims: The sources do not show that AmeriCorps and all federal national-service programs were terminated in March 2025.
The grant and workforce reductions are not proof that every AmeriCorps program or service placement ended permanently.
access_notes: Both Reuters reports returned readable excerpts. The April 25 $400 million figure is attributed to a Washington Post report; the April 29 workforce reduction appears in the states' lawsuit allegations.
narrow_corrected_title: Trump Administration Moves to Cancel Nearly $400 Million in AmeriCorps Grants
narrow_corrected_claim: In late April 2025, Reuters reported that DOGE ordered cancellation of about $400 million in AmeriCorps grants and that states sued over grant terminations and major workforce cuts. This documents severe reductions and litigation, not the March termination of AmeriCorps and every national-service program.
exact_remaining_gap: The cited reports do not establish that all AmeriCorps programs or all federal national-service programs were permanently ended; the lawsuit's allegations and final court outcome require separate treatment.

supported_facts: A House Oversight investigation estimated that foreign governments paid about $3.7 million to the Trump International Hotel in Washington from 2017 through 2020.
The committee said the payments raised possible Foreign Emoluments Clause concerns; this was a committee estimate and argument, not a court finding.
unsupported_original_claims: The reviewed source does not support attributing a '$4M+' estimate specifically to CREW for the D.C. hotel.
The source does not establish that a court found unconstitutional emoluments or that every payment included in the estimate was unlawful.
access_notes: The House Oversight Committee release returned readable text with the estimate, date range, and attribution.
narrow_corrected_title: House Oversight Estimates $3.7 Million in Foreign-Government Payments to Trump D.C. Hotel
narrow_corrected_claim: A House Oversight investigation estimated that foreign governments paid about $3.7 million to the Trump International Hotel in Washington from 2017 through 2020. The committee said the payments raised possible constitutional concerns; the estimate is not a judicial finding.
exact_remaining_gap: The cited committee release does not validate CREW's alleged $4M-plus D.C.-hotel estimate or establish a constitutional violation; the source and scope of the frozen attribution remain unverified.

supported_facts: WIRED reported in April 2025, citing court filings, that DOGE affiliates had access to 19 sensitive HHS systems; it said one instance appeared to lack required security training.
The Washington Post reported that HHS granted DOGE associates read-only access to a sensitive child-support database containing income data, over career employees' objections.
unsupported_original_claims: The reviewed reports do not establish unrestricted access to complete medical records for millions of people or access to HIV status, mental-health diagnoses, and prescription histories as claimed.
The articles do not establish that all access lacked legal authorization or patient consent, or that standard controls were universally bypassed.
access_notes: WIRED and Washington Post article excerpts returned readable text. Their described systems and case concern do not establish blanket access to complete clinical records.
narrow_corrected_title: Reporting Describes DOGE Access to Sensitive HHS Systems and a Child-Support Database
narrow_corrected_claim: Reporting based on HHS court filings said DOGE affiliates had access to 19 sensitive HHS systems, with one instance apparently lacking required training. The Washington Post separately reported read-only DOGE access to a child-support database containing income information. These reports do not establish unrestricted access to complete medical records for millions of Americans.
exact_remaining_gap: The sources do not substantiate the frozen claims about complete clinical records, specific diagnoses and prescriptions, universal authorization failures, or carte-blanche access.

supported_facts: USCIS describes an alien-registration requirement for certain noncitizens age 14 or older who were not previously registered and fingerprinted when required and who remain in the United States for at least 30 days.

The registration process includes Form G-325R and fingerprints where legally required; it is not evidence of a new universal biometric database collecting DNA, iris scans, and facial geometry from every undocumented immigrant.
unsupported_original_claims: The USCIS page does not establish that DHS created a new database for every undocumented immigrant.
The source does not support universal collection of facial geometry, iris scans, and DNA, or the claim that records would be shared with authoritarian governments.
access_notes: The USCIS Alien Registration Requirement page returned readable text describing eligibility categories, registration, and fingerprint requirements.
narrow_corrected_title: USCIS Implements Registration and Fingerprinting Requirements for Certain Noncitizens
narrow_corrected_claim: USCIS describes registration requirements for certain previously unregistered noncitizens who remain in the United States for 30 days or longer; fingerprints are required where applicable under law. The cited process is not evidence of universal enrollment in a newly created DHS database or collection of DNA, iris scans, and facial geometry.
exact_remaining_gap: The USCIS page does not substantiate the frozen claims about a comprehensive new database, biometric modalities beyond applicable fingerprints, universal coverage, or foreign sharing.
